title: Oxalates: what they are, food sources, and calcium absorption

seo.title: Oxalates and calcium absorption: what foods matter
seo.meta_description: Oxalate can bind calcium and lower absorption. Only about 5% of spinach calcium is absorbed versus roughly 27% from milk, according to NIH.
seo.search_intent: Understand oxalates, food sources, and why calcium from some vegetables is absorbed poorly.

excerpt: Oxalates are natural compounds in many plants. They can bind calcium and form poorly soluble salts, reducing the fraction of calcium available for absorption. Spinach is the classic example: it contains a meaningful amount of calcium, but NIH estimates that only about 5% is absorbed, versus roughly 27% from milk. Lower-oxalate vegetables such as kale, broccoli and bok choy have much better calcium bioavailability.
content_html:
Spinach often appears on lists of calcium-containing foods, yet it is also the standard example of poorly absorbed plant calcium. Both statements can be true.

Oxalate can bind calcium inside a food and form salts that are difficult to absorb. That is why calcium content and calcium bioavailability are not the same number.

What oxalates are

Oxalic acid and its salts, oxalates, occur naturally in many plant foods. Amounts vary widely by species, variety, plant part and preparation.

Spinach puts numbers on the difference

NIH notes that calcium absorption from dairy and many fortified foods is around 30%. In the classic comparison, about 27% of milk calcium was absorbed versus only about 5% of spinach calcium.

So 100 mg of calcium from spinach is not nutritionally equivalent to 100 mg from milk or a well-formulated fortified beverage.

Not every calcium-containing vegetable has the same issue

FoodBioavailability context
SpinachHigh oxalate; low calcium absorption (~5%)
MilkApprox. calcium absorption ~27–30%
Kale, broccoli, bok choyLower levels of calcium-binding compounds; fractional absorption can be similar to milk

Low-oxalate vegetables may contain less calcium per serving than dairy, but the fraction absorbed can be high. Content and bioavailability therefore need to be considered together.

Does cooking remove oxalate?

Some soluble oxalate can move into cooking water. Boiling and discarding that water can reduce oxalate more than dry methods such as roasting, but the reduction varies widely among foods.

Does spinach oxalate block all calcium in a meal?

No. Meal interactions are more complicated than a one-to-one binding equation. Oxalate helps explain why spinach calcium itself is poorly absorbed, but it does not automatically make calcium from every other food in the meal unavailable.

The whole diet matters more than an “antinutrient” list

NIH notes that when people eat a varied diet, oxalic- and phytic-acid interactions probably have little overall nutritional consequence. The practical problem is relying on a very low-bioavailability food as a major calcium source.

The useful takeaway

Spinach can contain calcium and still be an inefficient calcium source. Dairy, fortified foods, canned fish with edible bones and lower-oxalate vegetables such as kale, broccoli and bok choy can provide more absorbable calcium.

faq.question: Does spinach contain calcium?
faq.answer: Yes, but much of it is poorly available because of oxalate. NIH estimates about 5% absorption from spinach versus roughly 27% from milk.

faq.question: Does oxalate remove calcium?
faq.answer: No. It can bind some calcium and reduce how much remains available for intestinal absorption.

faq.question: Does kale have the same problem as spinach?
faq.answer: Not to the same degree. Kale, broccoli and bok choy have much better calcium bioavailability and can approach milk in fractional absorption.
